lead: Every speech sound belongs to a small class. The class is fixed by two things: whether the vocal folds vibrate, and where and how the vocal tract narrows. Phonetics gives each class a name. Three labels — voicing, place, manner — name any consonant; three more — height, backness, rounding — name any vowel. Speech recognisers and synthesisers care because the phone set of a language is the unit they model. Language teachers and speech therapists use the same labels. This chapter builds the labels and reads them off English, Hindi and Tamil sounds.
prereq: You need: 7.1 for the lungs, the vocal folds and the vocal tract as a filter.

blocks.text: Air from the lungs rises through the larynx. The vocal folds there either vibrate or stay apart. Vibrating folds make a voiced sound; folds held apart make a voiceless sound. Say /s/ and then /z/ with a finger on your throat. /z/ buzzes and /s/ does not, and that buzz is their only difference.
Place of articulation is the point where the vocal tract narrows most. These nine places cover English and most Indian languages.

items: Bilabial: both lips — /p/, /b/, /m/
Labiodental: lower lip on upper teeth — /f/, /v/
Dental: tongue tip at the upper teeth — /θ/ in 'think', /ð/ in 'this'
Alveolar: tongue tip at the ridge behind the teeth — /t/, /d/, /s/, /z/, /n/, /l/
Retroflex: the tongue tip is curled back so that it touches (or the underside faces) the alveolar ridge and the region just behind it — Hindi ट /ʈ/, Tamil ட
Palato-alveolar: the tongue blade makes the narrowing just behind the alveolar ridge, on the way to the hard palate — /ʃ/ in 'ship', /tʃ/ in 'church'
Palatal: the front of the tongue body rises to the hard palate itself — /j/ in 'yes'
Velar: back of tongue at the soft palate — /k/, /g/, /ŋ/ in 'sing'
Glottal: narrowing at the vocal folds themselves — /h/

blocks.text: Ask 'where is the air squeezed?' and the answer is the place. Ask 'are the folds vibrating?' and the answer is the voicing. Two labels are done. The third is manner.

Manner is how the narrowing is made. Some syllabi call it the constriction type. Narrowing comes in three broad kinds: a full closure, a narrow gap that makes turbulence, and a free approach that makes none.

items: Stop (plosive): full closure, then a release — /p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/
Nasal: full closure in the mouth, air escapes through the nose — /m/, /n/, /ŋ/
Fricative: narrow gap, air hisses — /f/, /v/, /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /h/
Affricate: a stop released slowly into a fricative — /tʃ/ in 'church', /dʒ/ in 'judge'
Lateral: air flows around the sides of the tongue — /l/
Approximant: articulators approach, no turbulence — /w/, /j/
Tap or flap: one quick touch of the tongue — Hindi र /ɾ/
Trill: repeated vibration — Tamil ற, the rolled /r/ of many Indian languages
Decide voicing: is the buzz there or not?
Decide place: which two articulators are closest?
Decide manner: closure, hiss, or free flow?
Say the three labels in that order and you have named the consonant.

blocks.text: A complete label reads as voicing, then place, then manner. /b/ is a voiced bilabial stop. /s/ is a voiceless alveolar fricative.

In a vowel the mouth stays open and nothing closes. The tongue body moves up or down and forward or back, and the lips may round. Each of these changes the shape of the tube above the larynx, and so changes the sound.

items: Tongue height: close (high) to open (low)
Tongue backness: front to back
Lip rounding: rounded or unrounded

blocks.text: The vowel quadrilateral is a trapezoid standing for the mouth: front on the left, back on the right, close at the top, open at the bottom. Plot a vowel inside it and you have its height and backness.

items: /iː/ in 'beat': close front unrounded
/uː/ in 'boot': close back rounded
/æ/ in 'cat': open front unrounded
/ɑː/ in 'calm': open back unrounded
/ə/ in 'about': mid central unrounded

blocks.text: A phone is one actual sound, written in square brackets: [p]. A phoneme is a sound category that changes meaning, written in slashes: /p/. 'pat' versus 'bat' shows that English /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes. An allophone is a variant of one phoneme. English /p/ is aspirated [pʰ] in 'pin' and plain [p] in 'spin'; the two never separate words, so both are allophones of /p/.

A syllable is onset + nucleus + coda. The nucleus is usually a vowel. In 'cat', /k/ is the onset, /æ/ the nucleus, /t/ the coda. In 'speaks' /spiːks/, /s p/ is the onset, /iː/ the nucleus, /k s/ the coda.

items: Hindi stops come in fours at each place: voiceless /k/, voiceless aspirated /kʰ/ (ख), voiced /g/, voiced aspirated /gʰ/ (घ). Aspiration alone is a phoneme difference.
Hindi त /t̪/ and ट /ʈ/, and Tamil த and ட, keep dental and retroflex apart. English has only alveolar /t/, so many Indian speakers use the retroflex for it.

figure.caption: Follow a root-to-leaf path to get the three labels for each first sound. The /p/ and /b/ leaves share bilabial place and stop manner, so only voicing separates them; /m/ branches to nasal, not stop.

spec.aria: A decision tree groups the first sounds of pat, bat, mat, fat and sat: bilabial has /p/ stop, /b/ stop and /m/ nasal under voiceless and voiced; labiodental gives /f/ fricative; alveolar gives /s/ fricative.

examples.question: Classify the first sound of each of these five words: pat, bat, mat, fat, sat. For each, give voicing, place and manner. Then say how many of the five are voiceless and how many are voiced.
steps: 'pat' begins with /p/: folds apart, so voiceless; both lips, so bilabial; full closure released, so stop. Voiceless bilabial stop.
'bat' begins with /b/: same lips and same closure, but the folds vibrate. Voiced bilabial stop. So /p/ and /b/ differ only in voicing.
'mat' begins with /m/: voiced, bilabial, and air leaves through the nose, so nasal. Voiced bilabial nasal.
'fat' begins with /f/: voiceless, lower lip on upper teeth, so labiodental, with a hiss, so fricative. Voiceless labiodental fricative.
'sat' begins with /s/: voiceless, tongue tip at the ridge, so alveolar, with a hiss, so fricative. Voiceless alveolar fricative.
Count voiceless: /p/, /f/, /s/ give 3. Count voiced: /b/, /m/ give 2. Total 3 + 2 = 5 words, which matches.
Note the pairs. 'pat' and 'bat' differ only in voicing; 'pat' and 'fat' differ in place and manner together.
examples.answer: The five first sounds are: /p/ voiceless bilabial stop, /b/ voiced bilabial stop, /m/ voiced bilabial nasal, /f/ voiceless labiodental fricative, /s/ voiceless alveolar fricative; 3 of the five are voiceless and 2 are voiced.

traps: Calling /m/ a bilabial stop. The mouth is fully closed, but air still flows out through the nose, so the manner is nasal.
Swapping place and manner: /s/ and /t/ are both alveolar, and they differ in manner (fricative versus stop), not in place.
Trusting English spelling. 'ship' starts with one fricative /ʃ/, not /s/ + /h/; 'think' starts with dental /θ/, not /t/ + /h/; 'church' starts with the single affricate /tʃ/.
Mixing the brackets. [p] is one phone, /p/ is a phoneme, and [pʰ] and [p] are two phones of one English phoneme.
Reading Hindi /kʰ/ as 'k plus h'. It is one aspirated stop, released with a puff of air, and क versus ख is a meaning difference.

quiz.q: Name the three labels that together classify any consonant.
quiz.a: Voicing, place of articulation, manner of articulation.

quiz.q: Which two articulators form a labiodental sound?
quiz.a: The lower lip and the upper teeth, as in /f/ and /v/.

quiz.q: The lips close completely for /m/. Why is /m/ still not called a stop?
quiz.a: Because the closure is only in the mouth. The soft palate lowers and air escapes through the nose, so the manner is nasal, not stop.

quiz.q: Give the full three-label description of the first sound of 'judge' and of 'sing'.
quiz.a: 'judge' begins with /dʒ/: voiced, palato-alveolar, affricate. 'sing' begins with /s/: voiceless, alveolar, fricative.

quiz.q: Split 'splash' into onset, nucleus and coda.
English has one alveolar /t/, while Hindi and Tamil keep dental and retroflex /t/ apart. What does this predict for an Indian speaker of English?
quiz.a: Both native sounds map onto the single English category, so the speaker may use either, often the retroflex, for English /t/. An English listener hears one category and may not notice the difference, because the contrast is not phonemic in English.

quiz.q: In English, [pʰ] and [p] belong to one phoneme, but in Hindi /k/ and /kʰ/ are two. Explain the test that decides this.
quiz.a: Swap the two sounds in the same position and ask whether the meaning changes. In English [pʰ] and [p] never stand in the same environment: [pʰ] occurs word-initially or at the start of a stressed syllable, [p] after /s/. 'pin' [pʰɪn] and 'spin' [spɪn] differ in position (and in the preceding /s/), not in the vowel, so the two sounds never contrast and are allophones of one phoneme /p/. In Hindi, क and ख can stand in the same position (कल / खल) and the meaning changes, so /k/ and /kʰ/ are separate phonemes.

beyond: Not for the exam. The full International Phonetic Alphabet extends the same three labels to sounds English does not use, such as uvular and pharyngeal places, and adds diacritics for tiny differences. Pronunciation dictionaries used in synthesis list one phoneme string per word, and a forced aligner then matches that string to the recording. Modern neural models learn their own units from audio, but researchers still map those units back to phonemes to explain errors. Search for 'IPA chart', 'CMU pronouncing dictionary' and 'forced alignment' to go further.
